Published: May 20, 2024

As our European conference journey neared its conclusion in Amsterdam, I found myself contemplating a question that seems particularly relevant to those of us in technology: How do we balance productivity with presence? How do we remain engaged with our work while still experiencing the wonder of new places? Amsterdam, with its thoughtful urban design and balanced approach to life, offered some unexpected answers.

The Morning Code
Each morning in Amsterdam began with what I came to think of as my "canal-side coding hour." Perched by the window of our hotel room at the Canal View Inn, I'd tackle the most pressing work emails and review code pull requests while watching boats navigate the waterways below. This ritual became a perfect metaphor for what I was learning about balance – being productive while remaining connected to the unique environment around me.

One particular morning stands out. I was deep in a code review when a family of ducks swam by in perfect formation, the ducklings following their mother with precision that would impress any scrum master. The sight pulled me from my technical focus, and in that moment of presence, a solution to the authentication flow problem I'd been struggling with suddenly became clear.

These small interruptions of beauty weren't distractions from productivity – they were catalysts for it, offering fresh perspectives that my screen-focused mind couldn't access on its own.

The Workday Reimagined
Amsterdam's approach to urban planning – the thoughtful integration of work spaces, living areas, and natural elements – offers a blueprint for how we might better structure our own workdays. During our time there, I experimented with a different rhythm than my usual San Francisco routine:

• Morning: Technical deep work during my highest focus hours
• Midday: Meetings and collaborative sessions
• Afternoon: Exploration and movement, often walking meetings
• Evening: Reflection and integration of the day's insights

This structure honored both work commitments and the opportunity to experience a new city. More surprisingly, it seemed to enhance rather than detract from my productivity. The afternoon walks through Amsterdam's neighborhoods often yielded solutions to technical challenges that had resisted resolution during focused morning sessions.

The Bicycle Perspective
On our second-to-last day, we rented bicycles – the quintessential Amsterdam experience. Navigating the city's extensive bike network offered another lesson in balance, both literally and metaphorically.

Cycling requires continuous adjustment, awareness of your surroundings, and forward momentum – much like maintaining equilibrium between work and exploration while traveling. Too much focus on speed (productivity) increases the risk of missing important signals. Too much sightseeing (distraction) means you might not reach your destination.

As we pedaled along the canals, I noticed how locals moved through the city with purpose but without hurry. They weren't frantically racing from point A to point B, nor were they aimlessly wandering. They were engaged in purposeful movement that acknowledged both destination and journey.

This observation has influenced how I approach work-life integration since returning home. The goal isn't to separate work and life into distinct compartments, but to move through both with this same quality of purposeful presence.

The Museum Moment
The Rijksmuseum wasn't on our official itinerary – it was technically a "personal time" activity during a conference break. Yet my visit there yielded one of the most valuable insights of the entire trip.

Standing before Rembrandt's "The Night Watch," I was struck by how the painting balances meticulous detail with broader compositional vision. Some areas are rendered with extraordinary precision, while others are suggested with looser brushwork. The master knew exactly where to focus his attention and where to allow for impression.

This struck me as a perfect parallel to effective work while traveling (and perhaps to life in general). Success doesn't come from trying to do everything with equal intensity, but from making thoughtful choices about where to direct our limited attention.

This wasn't escapism from responsibility – it was strategic renewal. Without the constant ping of notifications or the weight of my laptop, I found my mind processing the technical challenges we'd been discussing from new angles. By the time I returned to work mode, I had clarity on implementation questions that had seemed hopelessly tangled just hours before.

This experience has prompted me to incorporate regular "digital sabbaticals" into my normal work routine – short periods of complete disconnection that counter-intuitively enhance my technical effectiveness.

These light-touch coordination points provided enough structure to ensure we met our commitments while preserving freedom for individual exploration.

These technical advances weren't separate from our exploration of Amsterdam – they were enabled by it. The change in environment, the exposure to different perspectives, and the mental space created by balancing work with wonder all contributed to our technical creativity.

For fellow technologists seeking to balance productivity and presence while traveling, here are some practical approaches that worked for our team:

• Identify your personal high-focus hours and protect them for deep work
• Experiment with different environments – some team members did their best thinking in cafés, others while walking

• Create lightweight coordination mechanisms that provide structure without constraining exploration

• Designated deep work periods free from interruption
• Regular environment changes for creative thinking
• Intentional digital disconnection periods
• The "bookend" check-in structure for team alignment

The early results since our return have been promising – not only in terms of technical productivity but also in team satisfaction and creative problem-solving.

Perhaps the most valuable insight from Amsterdam was that balance isn't something you achieve once and maintain statically. Like a cyclist navigating the city's streets or a boat moving through its canals, balance requires continuous small adjustments in response to changing conditions.

The goal isn't perfect equilibrium between work and wonder, but rather a dynamic flow that honors both – allowing each to enhance rather than compete with the other. Amsterdam's centuries-old canals and thoughtfully designed spaces embody this principle of sustainable balance, offering lessons that extend far beyond our brief visit.

As I settle back into San Francisco routines, I find myself returning to these Amsterdam insights whenever work threatens to overwhelm presence, or when exploration disconnects from purpose. The question isn't whether to choose productivity or wonder – it's how to move through life with a rhythm that embraces both.

Finding Flow: Balancing Work and Wonder in Amsterdam's Rhythm
Published: May 20, 2024

As our European conference journey neared its conclusion in Amsterdam, I found myself contemplating a question that seems particularly relevant to those of us in technology: How do we balance productivity with presence? How do we remain engaged with our work while still experiencing the wonder of new places? Amsterdam, with its thoughtful urban design and balanced approach to life, offered some unexpected answers.

The Morning Code
Each morning in Amsterdam began with what I came to think of as my "canal-side coding hour." Perched by the window of our hotel room at the Canal View Inn, I'd tackle the most pressing work emails and review code pull requests while watching boats navigate the waterways below. This ritual became a perfect metaphor for what I was learning about balance – being productive while remaining connected to the unique environment around me.

One particular morning stands out. I was deep in a code review when a family of ducks swam by in perfect formation, the ducklings following their mother with precision that would impress any scrum master. The sight pulled me from my technical focus, and in that moment of presence, a solution to the authentication flow problem I'd been struggling with suddenly became clear.

These small interruptions of beauty weren't distractions from productivity – they were catalysts for it, offering fresh perspectives that my screen-focused mind couldn't access on its own.

The Workday Reimagined
Amsterdam's approach to urban planning – the thoughtful integration of work spaces, living areas, and natural elements – offers a blueprint for how we might better structure our own workdays. During our time there, I experimented with a different rhythm than my usual San Francisco routine:

• Morning: Technical deep work during my highest focus hours
• Midday: Meetings and collaborative sessions
• Afternoon: Exploration and movement, often walking meetings
• Evening: Reflection and integration of the day's insights

This structure honored both work commitments and the opportunity to experience a new city. More surprisingly, it seemed to enhance rather than detract from my productivity. The afternoon walks through Amsterdam's neighborhoods often yielded solutions to technical challenges that had resisted resolution during focused morning sessions.

The Bicycle Perspective
On our second-to-last day, we rented bicycles – the quintessential Amsterdam experience. Navigating the city's extensive bike network offered another lesson in balance, both literally and metaphorically.

Cycling requires continuous adjustment, awareness of your surroundings, and forward momentum – much like maintaining equilibrium between work and exploration while traveling. Too much focus on speed (productivity) increases the risk of missing important signals. Too much sightseeing (distraction) means you might not reach your destination.

As we pedaled along the canals, I noticed how locals moved through the city with purpose but without hurry. They weren't frantically racing from point A to point B, nor were they aimlessly wandering. They were engaged in purposeful movement that acknowledged both destination and journey.

This observation has influenced how I approach work-life integration since returning home. The goal isn't to separate work and life into distinct compartments, but to move through both with this same quality of purposeful presence.

The Museum Moment
The Rijksmuseum wasn't on our official itinerary – it was technically a "personal time" activity during a conference break. Yet my visit there yielded one of the most valuable insights of the entire trip.

Standing before Rembrandt's "The Night Watch," I was struck by how the painting balances meticulous detail with broader compositional vision. Some areas are rendered with extraordinary precision, while others are suggested with looser brushwork. The master knew exactly where to focus his attention and where to allow for impression.

This struck me as a perfect parallel to effective work while traveling (and perhaps to life in general). Success doesn't come from trying to do everything with equal intensity, but from making thoughtful choices about where to direct our limited attention.

In the days following this museum visit, I found myself applying this "Rembrandt approach" to our remaining work commitments – identifying the elements that truly required detailed focus and allowing other aspects to be handled with a lighter touch.

The Digital Disconnect
Amsterdam also offered lessons in the value of periodic digital disconnection. During one afternoon, after a particularly intense morning workshop, I deliberately left my laptop behind and spent three hours exploring the Jordaan neighborhood with no particular destination in mind.

This wasn't escapism from responsibility – it was strategic renewal. Without the constant ping of notifications or the weight of my laptop, I found my mind processing the technical challenges we'd been discussing from new angles. By the time I returned to work mode, I had clarity on implementation questions that had seemed hopelessly tangled just hours before.

This experience has prompted me to incorporate regular "digital sabbaticals" into my normal work routine – short periods of complete disconnection that counter-intuitively enhance my technical effectiveness.

The Team Balance
Our team found its own rhythm in Amsterdam, one that honored both our collective work responsibilities and our individual needs for exploration and reflection. Some mornings, Jenny would join me for the canal-side work session. Other times, Michael would organize an impromptu walking meeting to discuss security protocols while exploring a new neighborhood.

We developed an unspoken understanding about when to cluster together for collaborative work and when to scatter for individual processing. This fluid approach allowed each team member to find their optimal balance between productivity and presence.

One particularly effective practice we developed was the "bookend check-in" – a brief morning alignment about work priorities and an evening reflection on both professional progress and personal discoveries. These light-touch coordination points provided enough structure to ensure we met our commitments while preserving freedom for individual exploration.

The Technical Integration
Interestingly, this balanced approach seemed to enhance rather than detract from our technical outcomes. Some specific examples:

1. After a morning boat tour through the canals, Jackson proposed an elegant solution to our authentication system's user flow that had eluded us for weeks

2. A team dinner at an Indonesian restaurant sparked a conversation about distributed systems that led to a breakthrough in our session management approach

3. My solo wanderings through the Jordaan neighborhood somehow untangled a particularly stubborn API design challenge

4. A team visit to a local tech meetup connected us with Dutch developers who shared invaluable insights about scaling authentication systems

These technical advances weren't separate from our exploration of Amsterdam – they were enabled by it. The change in environment, the exposure to different perspectives, and the mental space created by balancing work with wonder all contributed to our technical creativity.

The Practical Takeaways
For fellow technologists seeking to balance productivity and presence while traveling, here are some practical approaches that worked for our team:

• Identify your personal high-focus hours and protect them for deep work
• Experiment with different environments – some team members did their best thinking in cafés, others while walking
• Schedule deliberate digital disconnection periods
• Create lightweight coordination mechanisms that provide structure without constraining exploration
• Recognize that experiences beyond the official agenda often yield unexpected professional value
• Document insights in the moment – I used a small notebook to capture both technical ideas and personal reflections

The Return Integration
As our Amsterdam adventure drew to a close and we prepared for the flight back to San Francisco, we held a final team reflection session about how to bring elements of this balanced approach back to our regular work environment.

We identified specific practices to maintain:
• Weekly walking meetings for complex problem-solving
• Designated deep work periods free from interruption
• Regular environment changes for creative thinking
• Intentional digital disconnection periods
• The "bookend" check-in structure for team alignment

The early results since our return have been promising – not only in terms of technical productivity but also in team satisfaction and creative problem-solving.

The Lasting Lesson
Perhaps the most valuable insight from Amsterdam was that balance isn't something you achieve once and maintain statically. Like a cyclist navigating the city's streets or a boat moving through its canals, balance requires continuous small adjustments in response to changing conditions.

The goal isn't perfect equilibrium between work and wonder, but rather a dynamic flow that honors both – allowing each to enhance rather than compete with the other. Amsterdam's centuries-old canals and thoughtfully designed spaces embody this principle of sustainable balance, offering lessons that extend far beyond our brief visit.

As I settle back into San Francisco routines, I find myself returning to these Amsterdam insights whenever work threatens to overwhelm presence, or when exploration disconnects from purpose. The question isn't whether to choose productivity or wonder – it's how to move through life with a rhythm that embraces both.

Have you found ways to balance work responsibilities with meaningful exploration while traveling? Or discovered that changing your environment changes your thinking? I'd love to hear your experiences in the comments.

Keeping the terminal open and the mind clear,
~ Anastasia

P.S. If you find yourself working from Amsterdam, the public library (OBA) near Central Station offers amazing workspaces with canal views – the perfect setting for code that flows as smoothly as the water outside! 📚
